preamble: Typing a date takes four seconds, so it's worth asking why Docs has a command for it at all. What you're about to insert isn't text that happens to look like a date — it's a chip that Docs knows *is* a date. It can be re-picked from a calendar later, it stays formatted consistently, and other people's documents read it the same way yours does. You're inserting an object, not characters.
generalization: Smart chips are the general pattern: Docs has a small family of things that look like text but carry meaning underneath — dates, people, files, places. The tell is that you reach them through Insert rather than by typing. Anything you can type, you can type wrong; anything you insert, Docs keeps track of for you.

steps.intent: Nothing here is about changing text that already exists, so the formatting menus are the wrong family. You're putting a new object into the document at your cursor — that's one menu's entire job.
hints: Ask what kind of action this is: changing something already on the page, or adding something that isn't there yet.
The Insert menu, in the menu bar along the top.

wrongHints.Format: Format changes the appearance of text that's already in the document. Nothing has been added yet, so there's nothing for it to work on.
wrongHints.Edit: Edit is for moving existing content around — cut, copy, paste, find. A date chip doesn't exist yet to be edited.

steps.intent: Date isn't in the top level of this menu, and that tells you something: Docs doesn't treat it as an ordinary insertable object like an image or a table. It belongs to a small family of items that look like text but carry data underneath. Open the group that holds them.
hints: You're looking for the group of things that sit inline with your writing but aren't really writing — a person, a file, a date.
'Smart chips', in the upper half of the Insert menu.

wrongHints.Building blocks: A reasonable guess — building blocks are also prefabricated content. But those are whole templates dropped into the page, like a meeting-notes layout. A date sits inside a line of text.
wrongHints.Table: Tables structure a region of the page. You want a single item at the cursor.

steps.intent: Here's the family: people, files, calendar events, dates. Each one is a chip that stays connected to what it represents. Pick Date, and Docs will offer you a calendar to choose from rather than asking you to type digits.
hints: Of the chips listed, only one refers to a point in time rather than a person, a file, or a place.
'Date', partway down the submenu that just opened to the right.

wrongHints.Place: Places are locations on a map. Close in spirit — both are chips — but the wrong kind of fact.

steps.intent: The calendar that appeared is the point of doing it this way: you're choosing a date rather than spelling one. Nothing lands in the document until you confirm the choice, so finish it.
hints: The picker is waiting on you — it wants a decision, not another selection.
The confirm button at the bottom of the date picker.
